effect_estimate.comment: Synthesizes exact quantitative results from the chronometric time-measurement study (n = 56) and questionnaire survey (N = 97; N = 90 in regressions) alongside qualitative thematic findings (n = 30) linking symmetrical fixture standards, missing care infrastructure, fees, and fragmented governance to unequal sanitation access.
effect_estimate.value: In chronometric observations (n = 56; 24 men, 32 women), women spent ~15-20 s longer using public restrooms than men, with a mean duration of 136.63 s (range 73-231 s; peak-period mean 181.67 s) for women versus 121.25 s (range 31-228 s; peak-period mean 131 s) for men (Table 4 reports rounded ~159 s vs. ~126 s). In questionnaire comparisons (N = 97, Welch's ANOVA), women reported lower perceived safety (mean 2.39 [SD 0.967] vs. 3.26 [SD 1.059], F(1, 43.7) = 13.89, p < 0.001), more frequent inability to change a child's nappy due to missing changing facilities (coded 1 = yes, 2 = no: mean 1.57 [SD 0.498] vs. 1.81 [SD 0.396], F(1, 59.2) = 6.33, p = 0.015), greater importance of unisex toilets (mean 2.71 [SD 1.416] vs. 1.67 [SD 0.920], F(1, 72.4) = 18.30, p < 0.001), and stronger agreement that public buildings need more women's toilets (reverse-interpreted coding: mean 1.44 [SD 0.828] vs. 2.52 [SD 1.252], F(1, 35.1) = 17.06, p < 0.001; OLS gender b = -0.920, SE = 0.281, p = 0.002, R2 = 0.238, N = 90), while both genders similarly attributed women's toilet queues to architectural/design problems (F(1, 95) = 3.75, p = 0.056). Fewer reported adverse toilet experiences predicted higher satisfaction/perceived safety (r = 0.33, p = 0.001; OLS b = 0.382, SE = 0.156, p = 0.016, R2 = 0.135, N = 90) and mediated older age's negative indirect effect on satisfaction (indirect effect = -0.237, SE = 0.095, 95% CI [-0.439, -0.071], p = 0.012). Qualitative narratives (n = 30) highlighted privacy breaches, hygiene deficits, paid/commercial workarounds, care burdens, and long queues.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 6-8, Section 3.1 and Table 2; PDF p. 8-9, Section 3.2 and Table 3; PDF p. 9-10, Section 3.3 and Table 4

mechanism_certainty.comment: Design ceiling is 2 (MMAT mixed-methods study). Assigned 1 because the empirical components document descriptive and statistical associations among gender, restroom use duration, user-reported service deficits (lack of nappy-changing facilities, paid access, queues, hygiene/privacy issues), and perceived safety/satisfaction, while the underlying legal, regulatory, and administrative accountability mechanisms (state building codes, municipal network planning, operator closure/maintenance policies, and external queue formation) were doctrinally analyzed and inferred rather than directly observed empirically (waiting time outside restrooms was not recorded, PDF p. 6).
